Compared with some of the traditional natural sciences, acoustics is a young discipline. It took shape as a formal field only in the mid-to-late nineteenth century, a mere 150 or 160 years ago. In China, acoustics as a discipline began in the 1950s with four academicians, Dezhao Wang, Dayou Ma, Rongjue Wei and Chongfu Ying (corrected, with thanks to @Liu Tone), so it is only a few decades old. Whether you look internationally or within China, acoustics has not been developing for long.

A blog post on ScienceNet (sciencenet.cn)

Young as it is, the field covers an enormous range and cuts across countless other disciplines. At an acoustics conference you meet people from every kind of background, some of whom may not be able to talk to one another at all.

In China’s automotive industry, NVH has only taken off in the past ten years or so, and the prospects are good. Every major carmaker has an NVH department. As the traditional car industry declines and electric vehicles rise, automotive acousticians have even more room to work. An electric car differs from a combustion-engine car in its motor, its structure and many of its components, so NVH faces new challenges. The overall SPL drops considerably, but high-frequency motor noise, tire noise and wind noise stand out because the engine no longer masks them, and a car that is too quiet is a potential danger to pedestrians. These are all problems NVH engineers have to consider and solve.

Another big area is voice interaction. From speech capture with microphone arrays, through speech recognition and semantic analysis, to speech synthesis at the end of the chain, it draws on a great deal of acoustics. Its links with artificial intelligence, machine learning and big data make it a very attractive field, too, although personally I’m not very optimistic about voice as a mode of interaction.

Take Google’s AudioSet, for example:

AudioSet consists of an expanding ontology of 632 audio event classes and a collection of 2,084,320 human-labeled 10-second sound clips drawn from YouTube videos.

Very cool.


Then there are the other areas. Traditional architectural acoustics, from concert hall design to noise control and sound insulation, needs no introduction. There is 3D reproduction combined with VR, for example in headphones and loudspeakers, or 3D sound to go with VR broadcasts. There is Goertek, one of China’s earliest acoustics companies, which is active in many fields, including headphone and speaker manufacturing, smart voice and VR/AR. And a few companies are working on active noise control.

In short, acoustics in China is young and carries little weight internationally, but like China’s other industries it has shot up out of nowhere and is developing strongly. When I finished my master’s degree, there were almost no acoustics companies to apply to; now companies have sprung up in every subfield. Given how few people work in acoustics, the job prospects for acoustics students are fairly good.

For more on acoustics and its applications, see my Zhihu column:
